name: Rosa Hansen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Rosa. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think. Is that all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: That's fine. I'll be honest with you, I'm not a fan of all this AI talk, so you might get some grumbling. But I'm happy to help.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at the Harbour Street Health Centre, a public clinic in a part of town where a lot of people work shifts and a lot of people don't work at all. I start at eight with a stack of blood results and letters, then it's patients every ten minutes until lunch, which I usually eat standing at the printer. Afternoons are more patients, home visit calls and phone appointments. I love the moment someone finally tells you what's really wrong, usually right as they stand up to leave. What wears me out is the paperwork and the feeling that ten minutes is never enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, I told you so. At our staff meetings people keep saying AI will fix the waiting list, and I'd be the one saying the waiting list was never a software problem. It's a staffing problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means my life stays exactly as hard as it is now. We're short two doctors at Harbour Street and nobody's applied for the posts in eight months. I'm tired already, and I'm only three years into this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep turning up, keep my patient list, and keep pushing the union on safe patient numbers. I'd also keep putting a few hundred a month into savings, because rent on our flat went up again in spring. Nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved about the AI part, but it's not a happy picture. It's the same grind with nobody coming to rescue us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're tired already. What does that look like on a bad day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last Tuesday I saw thirty-four people and wrote my last referral at half seven at night. My partner Tomas had made dinner and it was cold by the time I got in. I sat in the car outside the flat for ten minutes before I could go up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you push the union for, exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A cap on how many patients one doctor sees in a day, and money to fill the empty posts. The routine bits AI might do, like sorting letters, are nice, but they're not the reason I go home exhausted. The ten-minute slot is the reason.

say: I'd tell colleagues that **AI hype** was never going to fix a staffing problem.
I'd say Harbour Street needs **two more doctors**, not new software.
think: I think my life stays as **hard as now**, with two empty posts and long days.
I worry about **burning out** only three years into the job.
do: Keep my **patient list** and push the union for a cap on daily patients.
Keep putting **a few hundred** a month into savings after the spring rent rise.
feel: She feels **relieved** about AI but **worn down** by the same grind.
S0.quote: The routine bits AI might do, like sorting letters, are nice, but they're not the reason I go home exhausted. The ten-minute slot is the reason.
fieldNote: Her **pressure** is staffing and workload, not technology, so AI Plateau changes little for her.
Her income is **secure**, but she is already close to burnout at 27.
She frames everything through the **union** and safe patient numbers.

steps.text: Push the doctors' union for a daily cap on patients per doctor
Keep seeing the same patient list at Harbour Street
Put a few hundred a month into savings after the rent rise

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say: who checks the machine? If software is writing my referral letters and sorting who gets seen, I want to know who is responsible when it gets one wrong. I'd post that in the union group for sure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think management would use it as an excuse to cut appointment times even further. They'd say the AI writes the notes, so you can see eight patients an hour now. And they'd hire fewer doctors, not more, so my job stays but gets worse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to every union meeting about it and try to get rules written down before the software comes in, not after. I'd probably have to learn the system they force on us, but I'd be slow and grumpy about it. I'd also try to save a bit harder, maybe stop the takeaway on Fridays, in case my hours get cut to make the numbers work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy is too soft a word. I feel like something I trained eleven years for is being turned into a production line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our receptionists, honestly. Joyce has been on the front desk for twenty years and she knows every family by name. If an AI answers the phones and books the slots, she's the first to go, and she's the one who notices when an old man sounds confused.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your job stays but gets worse. Could your pay or hours change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They could. If the clinic is paid per patient and the software lets them squeeze more in, they might move some of us to part-time contracts and fill gaps with remote doctors on screens. I don't think I'd lose the job, but I could lose a day a week.

say: I'd ask publicly **who is responsible** when the software gets a referral wrong.
I'd post in the **union group** that rules must come before the software.
think: I think management would use AI to **cut appointment times** even further.
My job likely stays, but I could lose **a day a week** to part-time contracts.
do: Go to every **union meeting** and push for written rules before rollout.
Learn the **forced system** slowly, only because I'd have to.
Cut the **Friday takeaway** and save harder in case my hours shrink.
feel: She feels her eleven years of training are being turned into a **production line**.
S1.quote: I feel like something I trained eleven years for is being turned into a production line.
fieldNote: She expects to keep the job but fears **lost hours** and a faster patient conveyor.
She worries about the **receptionist** before herself, a sign of her values.
Her resistance to tech is **principled**, not only habit: she wants accountability first.

steps.text: Push the union for written rules on clinic AI before it arrives
Learn the clinic's new note software only when it's required
Stop the Friday takeaway and add the money to savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment governments have to step in, full stop. You can't let a handful of tech firms take over the thinking part of medicine in two years. I'd be signing petitions and probably standing outside the health ministry with a placard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, I think most of what I do sitting at the desk, listening, deciding, writing it up, a machine could do by 2028 if it's that good. The examining, the injections, the smear tests, that's hands-on, so maybe I'd have until 2031 before robots do those. That's not a career, that's a countdown.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop thinking of savings as a cushion and treat them as the thing that gets us through. We have about four months put aside, so I'd stop spending on anything but rent and food. I'd lean on the union to fight for doctors to stay in the room, and I'd ask my parents if we could move back in with them if it came to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, mostly. And angry, because nobody asked us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a countdown. What would you tell Tomas that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him we can't sign the new lease on the bigger flat. My partner Tomas fixes buses for the city, and with robots three years behind, his job lasts a bit longer than mine might. A bus mechanic being safer than a doctor is a strange thing to say out loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn the AI tools to stay useful?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know. Part of me says I should, and part of me says that's just training my replacement. If the clinic made it a condition of keeping my job, I'd do it, but I wouldn't volunteer.

say: I'd say **governments must step in** before tech firms take over medicine.
I'd sign petitions and protest outside the **health ministry**.
think: I think AI could do my **desk work** by 2028, leaving only hands-on tasks.
Robots by 2031 make my career feel like a **countdown**.
do: Cut spending to **rent and food** and protect our four months of savings.
Back the **union fight** to keep doctors in the consulting room.
Ask my parents whether we could **move back in** if needed.
feel: She feels **frightened** and **angry** that no one asked doctors.
S2.quote: My partner Tomas fixes buses for the city, and with robots three years behind, his job lasts a bit longer than mine might.
fieldNote: She sees clearly that her **thinking work** goes first and her hands-on tasks buy only three years.
She is **torn** between learning AI and refusing to train her replacement.
Her plan rests on **family** and the union, not on changing herself.

steps.text: Cut spending to rent and food only
Join union protests to keep doctors in the consulting room
Ask her parents if they could move back in

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before really, but I'd have more time to organise. I'd say doctors and nurses need to be at the table writing the rules, and I'd say it in the local paper if they'd print me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With five years, I think the system would quietly plan around us. They'd stop training new family doctors around 2029 and keep the ones they have until the machines are ready. I'd still be working in 2031, but I'd be the person checking the machine's homework.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push the union to get a deal in writing: no doctor loses their post without retraining paid for. I'd probably take the sexual health and minor procedures course I've put off, because hands-on work buys me those extra three years. And we'd save for the flat deposit more slowly and keep the money where we can reach it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Less panicky than two years, but it's a slow dread instead of a sudden one. I don't like either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the procedures course now and not before?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I hate change, and before it didn't matter. Fitting coils, cutting out moles, that kind of work. If the thinking part goes in 2031 and the hands go in 2034, then being good with my hands is worth three years of rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The holiday we've been planning to Tomas's family. We'd go for a weekend instead of two weeks. It's small, but it would feel like admitting something.

say: I'd say **doctors and nurses** must help write the rules.
I'd write to the **local paper** if they'd print me.
think: I think the system would **stop training** new family doctors around 2029.
I'd still work in 2031, but mostly **checking the machine**.
do: Push the union for a **written deal** on paid retraining before any job loss.
Take the **minor procedures** course I've avoided for years.
Swap a two-week trip for a **weekend** and keep savings easy to reach.
feel: She feels a **slow dread** rather than sudden fear.
S3.quote: Being good with my hands is worth three years of rent.
fieldNote: The five-year warning moves her from protest to a **practical plan**.
She grasps the **three-year gap** between AI and robots and acts on it.
She is resistant, so even small changes feel like **admitting defeat**.

steps.text: Push the union for paid retraining written into every contract
Take the coil fitting and minor surgery course
Shorten the family holiday to a weekend and save the rest

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have a decade, so there's no excuse for governments not to plan. Public health care should own these systems, not rent them from private companies. I'd keep saying that until people are sick of me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years feels long enough to pretend it isn't coming, and that's what worries me. I'll be 37. Most of my career would be before it, but the second half is a blank page.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the procedures course in the next couple of years, not in a panic. I'd stay active in the union and push for public ownership of the AI the clinic uses. I'd keep my job at Harbour Street, and we'd still try to buy a small flat, just a cheaper one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a low, background way. Like knowing the boiler is old.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a blank page. What would you want on it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to still be the person in the room. Even if a machine knows more than me, someone frightened wants a hand on their arm. I'd like that to be a real job, paid properly, not a volunteer role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about kids differently with a decade's notice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. Tomas and I said maybe at 32. I'd still want them, but I'd want to know my income is safe first, and in this picture I can't promise that.

say: I'd say a decade leaves **no excuse** for governments not to plan.
I'd argue **public health care** should own these systems.
think: I think ten years is long enough for people to **pretend** it isn't coming.
At 37, the second half of my career is a **blank page**.
do: Take the **procedures course** within two years, calmly.
Push the union for **public ownership** of clinic AI.
Still buy a flat, just a **cheaper one**.
feel: She feels a **low, background** anxiety, like an old boiler.
S4.quote: Even if a machine knows more than me, someone frightened wants a hand on their arm.
fieldNote: She expects her income to be **at risk** by her late thirties, even with time.
She would plan **calmly** but still hedges on having children.
Her hope is a paid, **human role** in care, protected by public ownership.

steps.text: Take the minor procedures course within two years
Campaign through the union for publicly owned clinic AI
Look for a cheaper flat to buy instead of the bigger one

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, no question. Two years isn't enough for anyone to fight for rules, and the thinking part of my job would just go. What would help is a law that a doctor stays responsible for every patient, and money for retraining that doesn't come out of our own pockets.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the patients. Everyone asks what happens to doctors, but the old woman who can't use a phone app is the one who gets lost in all of this.

headlineQuote: A bus mechanic being safer than a doctor is a strange thing to say out loud.
portrait: Rosa is a **27-year-old** family doctor at a busy public clinic, already tired from short staffing.
She is **union-minded** and wants rules and accountability before any AI reaches patients.
She never uses AI and would only learn it if **forced**, fearing she'd train her replacement.
Her mood rises from **uneasy** to alarmed as the AGI date gets closer.
She leans on **hands-on skills** and family to buy time, not on new technology.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because there'd be no time to fight for rules before her thinking work goes.
whatWouldHelp: A law keeping a **doctor responsible** for every patient.
**Retraining money** that doesn't come from doctors' own pockets.
